claims.claim: Cloudflare's hosted Storage Relay Service (SRS) monitors changes to SQLite's write-ahead log by hooking SQLite's VFS, and uploads them to object storage in batches of up to 10 seconds or 16 MB, whichever comes first.

On 20 August 2024 AWS announced S3 conditional writes with If-None-Match: a write that succeeds only if no object exists at that key; AWS said customers no longer need to build client-side consensus mechanisms to coordinate such updates. When several conditional creates race on one key, one succeeds and the others fail with a precondition error.

On 25 November 2024 AWS added If-Match conditional writes: S3 checks that the object's ETag still matches the value in the request before committing an overwrite, letting workloads offload compare-and-swap operations to S3.
A conditional write is applied only if the storage-side precondition holds for that write; the condition is checked by the store, not by the client.
workerd guards replacement of an ownership record with an opaque version (Guard::Match) or requires absence (Guard::Absent); here the ETag-like version is an opaque guard, not a content checksum.

Vogels describes how S3 built strong consistency internally: a cache coherence protocol for its metadata caches, new replication logic that lets S3 reason about the order of operations per object, and a witness component that is told about every change to an object, which acts like a read barrier so a cache learns whether its view is stale.

Vogels writes that S3 verified the design with integration tests, deductive proofs of the cache coherence algorithm and model checking, later extended to runnable code, and that this verification was more work than the implementation itself.

Inference: the application fleet relies on the store's conditional serialisation instead of running its own consensus service for ownership; the coordination still exists, inside the storage service (SB03, SB04).

claims.claim: In workerd each Durable Object has one owner record, do/<namespace>/<actor>/own.json, described in the code as the only authority for who owns it and whose log holds its latest commits. It holds three fields: node, epoch and from.

In workerd, from is the last epoch that opened. A claim writes the next epoch and copies from unchanged; the opening write sets from equal to the epoch. An epoch is still recovering while from differs from epoch, and it recovers from's log.

workerd's acquire_or_route: a record with no owner, or naming an instance whose lease expired, is taken over with the next epoch by a conditional write, so exactly one claimant wins; a record naming a live peer sends the request to that peer instead.

workerd lease constants: lease 20,000 ms; renewal every 3,000 ms, each bounded at 4,000 ms; a failed renewal retried every 1,000 ms; maximum clock skew 2,000 ms; safety margin twice the skew, 4,000 ms.
In workerd a lease holds at time now only if now plus the 4,000 ms safety margin is before its expiry; an actor serves only while it holds.

Before each renewal workerd fences if the node's clock is more than 2,000 ms off the bucket's, or if the lease would not still hold 4,000 ms from now (a paused process or blocked loop may have been taken over and must not renew and serve on).

Inference from holds and before_renew: with an expiry at 20,000 ms, the node may serve only while its clock reads below 16,000 ms and may start a renewal only below 12,000 ms. These are arithmetic boundaries, not guaranteed timer delivery.

workerd measures each node's skew against the bucket's observed clock; when no observation is available the skew defaults to zero, so the bound is an assumption rather than verified synchronisation.

celld leases default to a 10,000 ms lifetime renewed after one third of it; when the published expiry passes the node fences itself, stopping each active cell and failing incomplete requests, writes nothing, and exits with code 3; celld also checks the published expiry on every routed request.
celld's acknowledgement check after a bucket proof consults the ownership record rather than a clock, so neither a paused process nor a skewed clock can satisfy it.

In workerd, from is the last epoch that opened. A claim writes the next epoch and copies from unchanged; the opening write sets from equal to the epoch. An epoch is still recovering while from differs from epoch, and it recovers from's log.
In workerd a claimant that dies mid-recovery leaves from unchanged, so the next claimant still recovers the last epoch that actually opened.

workerd opens a claimed epoch only if the record still names this node at this epoch and from has not yet been set to it; the guarded write sets from to the epoch. If the record changed, the epoch never opens.

On takeover workerd deletes the node's non-authoritative local database, restores the recovering epoch's session from the bucket, uploads the starting snapshot of the new session, and only then performs the conditional open; if the record was superseded first, the epoch fails with "superseded before it opened".

SQLite's write-ahead log begins with a 32-byte header; each frame is a 24-byte frame header followed by one page; in a commit frame the header records the size of the database in pages after the commit, and is zero in other frames.

On 26 September 2024 Cloudflare put SQLite inside Durable Objects, running in the very same thread as the application; Kenton Varda wrote that this makes latency effectively zero, since nothing separates the application from SQLite. This describes local access, not end-to-end durable acknowledgement.

workerd's capture reads the writes SQLite makes to its WAL, as workerd's VFS reports them, and cuts them into transactions: frames since the last commit are buffered, and the write that completes a commit frame completes one transaction.

In workerd's capture a write at offset 0 starts a new WAL after a checkpoint copied earlier frames into the database file, and a rolled-back transaction's frames are overwritten by the next transaction's.

workerd stores each object's log in the bucket as gzipped files: batches log/<session>/<end> with runs of page frames merged to the newest version of each page, and snapshots snapshot/<session>/<frame>, in its own frames.capnp format.
Every workerd log file is gzipped; gzip ends with the content's CRC-32 and length, which the decoder checks, so a corrupt or truncated copy fails to replay rather than replaying wrong or short.
celld captures SQLite WAL changes into the LTX format (transaction ranges and page checksums); workerd's cluster path uses frames.capnp instead. The two implementations are distinct.
In workerd each epoch writes its own session of the object's log, starting with a snapshot of the state it inherited.

workerd snapshots a session when the log since the last snapshot has reached the database's size, keeping bucket writes within about twice the log, and uploads a replacement snapshot before deleting the files it covers.
workerd: a commit is acknowledged once the bucket holds it and own.json still names the epoch after the upload.

workerd's push stages the captured frames, uploads them, rereads the current epoch from own.json, and if it no longer matches returns "epoch was superseded" without acknowledging; only a match advances the acknowledgement.
workerd's code describes the epoch reread as "the re-read after a bucket upload that makes the upload an acknowledgement".

In workerd cluster mode local SQLite completion is not the acknowledgement: the commit waits for bucket-backed coverage. At both inspected workerd snapshots the commit path acknowledges after the upload and epoch reread; no follower acknowledgement path is present.

celld holds each response until a durability proof covers every write it can reveal: write responses, read-only responses when an uncovered committed write exists, error responses, R2 mutations, raw TCP actions, and each chunk of a streamed body.

celld must run under a supervisor that restarts it without an attempt limit and waits at least one lease lifetime between attempts; a fenced node exits and the fleet loses that capacity until restart.
Inference: lease expiry, guarded ownership updates and the post-upload epoch check close different failure windows; none of them alone suffices.

workerd's push stages the captured frames, uploads them, rereads the current epoch from own.json, and if it no longer matches returns "epoch was superseded" without acknowledging; only a match advances the acknowledgement.
celld: before restoring, a takeover seals the previous node-log session, so an outdated owner can no longer finish another fleet proof.

In workerd's capture a write at offset 0 starts a new WAL after a checkpoint copied earlier frames into the database file, and a rolled-back transaction's frames are overwritten by the next transaction's.
Restore replays recorded pages; it does not re-run application handlers.
At the supplied commit workerd clustering is experimental (Config.cluster behind --experimental) and lacks alarms; it is a beginning, not full platform parity.

The workerd cluster integration test starts a fake S3 and several workerd instances and exercises consistent state across instances (single-writer correctness), forwarding from the wrong instance, takeover after a node is killed and per-instance lease records; the later snapshot adds alarms on a survivor and facets. This film inspected these tests and did not execute them.
Inference: the alarm tests assert observed firings in specific kill-and-recover scenarios; they do not establish exactly-once external effects for arbitrary applications.

celld must run under a supervisor that restarts it without an attempt limit and waits at least one lease lifetime between attempts; a fenced node exits and the fleet loses that capacity until restart.
celld reserves bucket prefixes it reads to fence and restore cells; an operator must not delete, expire or overwrite objects there, so bucket lifecycle rules must not select them.
celld documents its supported APIs and limitations; running the runtime yourself does not establish full parity with the hosted platform.
The 2022 workerd post says workerd is not, on its own, a secure way to run possibly-malicious code; it must be enclosed in an additional sandboxing layer.

The commit message: several workerd processes form a cluster by sharing one S3-compatible bucket (Config.cluster, behind --experimental); each Durable Object has one owner at a time; requests reach it from any process; when its owner dies another process picks it up from the bucket; objects use the bucket as cold storage; for now a write is acknowledged only after it has been completely written to the bucket; alarms are not yet supported.
Alarms for clustered Durable Objects landed in workerd on 30 October 2026 (#8090) and facets on 31 October 2026 (#8113), both authored by Ryan Dahl; the later snapshot ad78a8fe includes alarm tests.
The joint post says Ryan Dahl and Bert Belder will lead a new effort to make self-hosting workerd a first-class supported way to build and run apps, bringing celld's code and ideas back into workerd.
Ryan Dahl writes that the team will put its future development into this shared platform rather than continuing a separate runtime.
Neither announcement states a purchase price or deal terms; the Cloudflare post carries an "Acquisitions" tag. The film does not describe terms.
Inference: serialising one ownership key does not by itself give atomic application transactions across separate objects.

Inference, matching celld's guarantees (a lost acknowledgement is not evidence that a write is absent): a lost reply cannot tell a client that a write did not happen, so durability alone does not give exactly-once effects on retry.

Inference: when the bucket is unreachable, no new upload-backed acknowledgements can complete, and sustained renewal failure fences the affected writers: safety is kept by stopping, not by serving on.
Inference: moving ownership serialisation into the bucket makes ownership progress depend on the bucket's semantics and availability.
